title: Why were the Spartans so formidable?
subtitle: The Spartan mirage
subject: histoire
description: Two kings, athletic girls, communal meals and an army all of Greece admired. Yet almost everything we know about Sparta comes from people who did not live there.
author: ezgi-gizem-berkay

hero.hook: Sparta has been admired for twenty-five centuries. Not one line of its history was written by a Spartan.

blocks.text: Sparta's social model keeps its share of mystery. The laws attributed to its lawgiver [[Lycurgus]] are said to have created a rare balance, in the sharing of property as in daily life. Plato drew on it for *The Republic*. But did this **2,500-year-old** ideal society really exist, or was it only a carefully built facade?

For twenty-five centuries, Sparta has served above all as a mirror for the ideals of each era. And none of that story comes from the Spartans themselves: written laws were forbidden there, and only fragments survive from **two poets**, Alcman and Tyrtaeus. No source describes Sparta from the inside.

According to ancient authors, Lycurgus studied history, philosophy and politics in Crete, Ionia and Egypt in the **9th or 8th century** BC, then reorganized the city. The [[Oracle of Delphi]] ratified his laws: this sacred endorsement is known as the "Great Rhetra." The accounts diverge so much that Plutarch, his Greek biographer, wrote: "Not a single thing can be said about him beyond dispute." For today's historians, this shadowy founder was later given the credit for centuries of institutional development.

blocks.caption: The temple of Apollo at Delphi, where the oracle is said to have ratified the laws of Lycurgus.

blocks.text: Seeking equality, Lycurgus set up a unique structure: **two kings** ruling together, a council of **thirty elders**, the gerousia, which also seated the kings, an assembly of citizens, the apella, and five inspectors elected each year, the [[ephors]]. The whole endured for a very long time without tyranny or civil war. Elsewhere in Greece, fearing one's rulers was dishonorable; in Sparta, obeying the law was a point of pride, and the thinkers of antiquity were fascinated by it.

Xenophon praised Lycurgus as a sage who taught citizens to prefer an honorable death to cowardice. Cowards even had a name, the tresantes, "those who tremble," and were kept at the margins of the city.

sections.title: Athletic girls, boys of the agoge, "Equals"

blocks.text: For Lycurgus, bearing children was women's first duty. So he required that they be educated, just like men. Girls competed in athletic contests, judged on agility and strength exactly like boys. And unlike **Athenian women**, Spartan women could acquire and inherit property.

blocks.caption: A young Spartan girl running: a bronze statuette kept at the British Museum.

blocks.text: Boys, for their part, went through state education, the [[agoge]]. Taken from their families at **seven**, they grew up under the supervision of upper-class adults, walked barefoot and wore the same single garment all year round.

Citizens called themselves the "Equals," homoioi. They ate modest communal meals, the [[syssitia]], designed for a balanced diet, avoided all ostentation and walked home afterward for exercise. It was also there that the young learned directly from the **elders**.

sections.title: An army built to hold down the helots

blocks.text: Sparta's heavy infantry was long regarded as the most disciplined army in the Greek world. Lycurgus built the state around a **permanent army**, which also shaped administration and production. Soldiers fought in a [[phalanx]], in squads and companies, wearing red tunics and carrying bronze shields. The army marched in order, set up camp by precise rules and trained without respite.

blocks.caption: Two ranks of heavy infantrymen, the hoplites, on the Chigi vase, around 650 BC.

blocks.text: Sparta was above all an infantry power. Its vital task: holding down the [[helots]], the enslaved population, far more numerous than the citizens. Every year the **ephors** formally declared war on them, and the young men of the [[krypteia]], secret units, spread fear by killing helots across the countryside.
The elite corps of the hippeis, whose name means "horsemen," fought on foot. Sparta had no regular cavalry until the late 5th century BC.

Leading its Peloponnesian allies since the **6th century** BC, Sparta finally defeated Athens in **404** BC. But its dominance over Greece lasted barely thirty years. In **371** BC, Thebes crushed it at Leuctra, freed the helots of Messenia and destroyed the city's economic base.

sections.title: The decline of a shrinking city

blocks.text: Contrary to popular belief, Sparta's downfall came from an internal contraction. Land was private, unequally distributed and inherited. Wealthy horse-breeders lived alongside citizens who could barely pay their share of the syssitia. And citizenship depended on that contribution: a man who lost his land lost his status. The number of citizens fell from **8,000** to fewer than **1,000** by Aristotle's time.

Women's rights over land served first of all the birth rate the state wanted. Without political rights, excluded from the apella and from public office, they could be shared among several men to produce healthy children. **Aristotle** saw a weakness in the fact that they owned **two-fifths** of the land, and noted that the Spartans, so strong in war, failed in peacetime.

blocks.text: Our picture of Sparta comes from Athenian admirers and critics, then from **Plutarch**, who wrote five centuries after the city's golden age. "Spartan history" is often no more than what was said about Sparta.
Sparta owed its strength to a permanent army designed to hold down the helots, and its fall to a body of citizens that kept shrinking. The rest is a mirage written by others.
